one_sentence: The paper introduces the Transformer, a translation model built only from attention layers (no recurrence or convolution), which trains faster and scores higher on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French than earlier models.

figures.why_it_matters: The full architecture: encoder stack on the left, decoder stack on the right, each built from attention and feed-forward sub-layers. This is the map for the whole method.
Zooms into the core operation: scaled dot-product attention (left) and how several of them run side by side as multi-head attention (right).
The argument for self-attention: compares cost per layer, sequential steps, and longest signal path against recurrent and convolutional layers.
The headline result: BLEU scores and training cost against earlier translation models on EN-DE and EN-FR.
The ablation study: what happens to quality when you change heads, key size, model size, dropout, label smoothing, or positional encoding.
Evidence the model works beyond translation: English constituency parsing scores.
Shows attention heads linking a word to a distant word in the same sentence, supporting the long-range dependency argument.
Two heads that appear to resolve what the pronoun 'its' refers to.
Different heads behave differently, suggesting they learn separate jobs.

prerequisites.why: The whole paper frames translation as turning one sequence into another: an encoder reads the input, a decoder writes the output one token at a time.
The approach the Transformer replaces. You need to see why stepping through words one by one blocks parallel training.
Before this paper, attention was an add-on to RNNs that let the decoder look back at input words. The paper makes it the only building block.
Attention scores are dot products between vectors, turned into weights that sum to 1 with softmax.
Inputs are tokens turned into vectors of size d_model = 512; tokens come from byte-pair encoding or word-pieces.
Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)); without knowing these, the architecture diagram is hard to read.
The translation quality metric used for every headline number. Higher is better.
Section 4 and Table 1 argue with O(n^2 d) versus O(n d^2) and path lengths.

simple.one_line: Instead of reading a sentence one word at a time, the computer lets every word look at every other word at once, and that works better and faster.

claims.simple: The new model only uses 'looking at other words'. It does not read words in order.
claims.analogy: Like a class where every student can talk to every other student at once, instead of passing a note down the row.

claims.simple: It translated English to German better than any model before it.
claims.analogy: Like a new runner beating the record, even beating relay teams.

claims.simple: On English to French, it was the best single model.
claims.analogy: Like winning the solo race, not the team race.

claims.simple: Even the small version beat older models and cost much less to train.
claims.analogy: Like a bike beating cars in a race while using no gas.

claims.simple: Any word can reach any other word in one step.
claims.analogy: Like a group chat instead of a game of telephone.

claims.simple: For normal sentence lengths, this way is also cheaper.
claims.analogy: Like a group chat being quick when the group is small.

claims.simple: They shrink big scores so learning does not get stuck.
claims.analogy: Like turning down a speaker that is so loud you cannot hear any detail.

claims.simple: Several small lookers beat one big looker, but too many is worse.
claims.analogy: Like a team of eight detectives, each checking different clues.

claims.simple: Making the 'matching keys' too small hurts.
claims.analogy: Like trying to match people using only one fact about them.

claims.simple: Two ways of telling the model word order worked about the same.
claims.analogy: Like numbering seats with a fixed pattern or letting kids pick numbers. Both work.

claims.simple: Bigger models did better, and randomly switching parts off during training helped.
claims.analogy: Like practising with one hand tied so you do not rely on one trick.

claims.simple: It also did well at a different job: drawing a sentence's grammar tree.
claims.analogy: Like a translator who also turns out good at diagramming sentences.

terms.simple: Deciding which other words matter most for this word.
Words in one sentence looking at each other.
The part that reads and understands the input sentence.
The part that writes the answer, one word at a time.
One looker. Many heads look for different things.
A tag on each word saying where it sits.
A score for how close a translation is to a human one.
